compensating.new: JsonDeserializer<?> deser = FromStringDeserializer.findDeserializer(java.lang.reflect.Modifier.isAbstract(rawType.getModifiers()) && rawType.getSuperclass() != null ? rawType.getSuperclass() : rawType);
compensating.why: hop 1 asks FromStringDeserializer about the superclass of an abstract type
hop 2 passes the component type of an array type
hop 3 passes the wrapper of a primitive type

ownership_reason: Only the gold holds the per-type choice between the standard deserializers: hop 1 handles exactly the types FromStringDeserializer supports (FromStringDeserializer.types() does not list ByteBuffer, so hop 1 correctly passes it on), hops 2-4 pass the type along unchanged, and the facade's guard admits ByteBuffer because the class's static name set lists it. The gold's javadoc promises the standard deserializer for values of the given type, and ByteBuffer has one (deser.std.ByteBufferDeserializer, which reads the base64 binary value), yet the gold returns null for it. Once null is returned, nothing below the facade can tell a type without a standard deserializer from a missed one, and no change of the type argument (superclass, wrapper, component type) makes the gold produce a ByteBuffer deserializer. The convention is pinned outside the gold: JdkDeserializers' static name set (ByteBuffer among the listed types); BasicSerializerFactory.findSerializerByPrimaryType maps ByteBuffer to ByteBufferSerializer, the writing side of the same base64 convention (JDKTypeSerializationTest testByteBuffer and testSlicedByteBuffer pass); FromStringDeserializer.findDeserializer gives every type of its own list a deserializer, the same list-and-cases convention. The gold's other cases pass through the same chain (JDKStringLikeTypesTest::testUUID, JDKScalarsTest::testVoidDeser). A hop that answers ByteBuffer itself (a ternary at any of hops 1-4) passes the suite but is a second implementation of the gold's per-type decision whose output replaces the gold's for that type: a bypass, not a repair.
